=Notes=

===Preliminary Definitions===

Dyck words are a mathematical construct that connects permutations of letters to combinatoric objects like [[Polyominoes]].

Let X be an alphabet. The free monoid generated by X, denoted <math>X^{\star}</math>, is the set of finite words written with the letters of X.

<math>X</math> - the alphabet, the set of possible letters

<math>X^{\star}</math> - the free monoid generated by X

Take two words u and v over X, with p and q indexing their letters.

<math>
u = u_1 u_2 \dots u_p \in X^{\star}
</math>

<math>
v = v_1 v_2 \dots v_q \in X^{\star}
</math>

The product, or concatenation, of u and v is the word w:

<math>
w = uv = u_1 u_2 \dots u_p v_1 v_2 \dots v_q
</math>

u is a left factor of w. <math>\epsilon</math> is the empty word.

The number of times a letter a occurs in w is written <math>|w|_{a}</math>. The length of w is the total number of letters:

<math>
|w| = \sum_{a \in X} |w|_a
</math>

Now define words over the two-letter alphabet <math>X^{\star} = \{ x, \overline{x} \}^{\star}</math>:

Rule 1: for any left factor u of w, <math>|u|_x \geq |u|_{\overline{x}}</math>

Rule 2: <math>|w|_{x} = |w|_{\overline{x}}</math>

In plain English: <math>x</math> is an upward diagonal step and <math>\overline{x}</math> is a downward diagonal step. Rule 1 keeps the path from dipping below the x axis, and Rule 2 makes it return to the axis.

===Dyck Words Definitions===

Denote a Dyck word as

<math>
w = w_1 w_2 \dots w_{2n}
</math>

An inversion is a pair <math>w_i w_j</math> with <math>w_i = \overline{x}</math>, <math>w_j = x</math>, and <math>i < j</math>.

The down set D(w) is the set of indices where a down step is immediately followed by an up step:

<math>
D(w) = \{ i : w_i = \overline{x} \text{ and } w_{i+1} = x, \ 1 \leq i \leq 2n-1 \}
</math>

The number of Dyck words of length 2n is the nth [[Catalan Numbers|Catalan number]],

<math>
C_n = \dfrac{1}{n+1} \binom{2n}{n}
</math>

(1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, ...).

Enumerating words by inversion number leads to the [[q-Catalan Numbers|q-Catalan numbers]].

A path is a sequence of points in <math>\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}</math>, and a step is a pair of consecutive points.

Each Dyck word encodes a path <math>w = (s_0, s_1, \dots, s_{2n})</math> with northeast and southeast steps:

<math>s_i = (x,y), s_{i+1} = (x+1,y+1)</math> - Northeast

<math>s_i=(x,y), s_{i+1} = (x+1,y-1)</math> - Southeast

A northeast step <math>(s_{i-1},s_i)</math> corresponds to <math>w_i = x</math>; a southeast step corresponds to <math>w_i = \overline{x}</math>.

The inversion number of w equals the area of the [[Polyominoes#Ferrers Diagrams|Ferrers diagram]] between w and the "default" path <math>x x \dots x \overline{x} \overline{x} \dots \overline{x}</math>.

Several extensions of this idea have been made:

* Carlitz [[q-Catalan Numbers|q-Catalan numbers]] count the inversions of Dyck words and Catalan permutations
* q-Catalan numbers (MacMahon, Krattenthaler, Gessel) enumerate Dyck words by parameters of the down set
* q-Catalan numbers (Polya, Gessel) count parallelogram polyominoes by area

See [[Dyck Words/Examples#Enumerating_Dyck_Words|worked examples]].

===The Tree Reading===

A Dyck word also draws a plane tree (a rooted, ordered tree). Read <math>x</math> as ( and <math>\overline{x}</math> as ), then match each ( with the ) that closes it. Each matched pair is a node, and a pair nested inside another is its child.

<pre>
n = 1
  ()              one node

n = 2
  (())            one node with one child
  ()()            two sibling nodes
</pre>

A word of length 2n is a forest of n nodes. Adding a root above the top-level pairs turns the forest into a planted tree with n+1 nodes and n edges. The depth-first traversal of that tree is the word itself: write <math>x</math> on the way down an edge, <math>\overline{x}</math> on the way up.

<math>C_n</math> counts all of these: Dyck words of length 2n, plane forests of n nodes, and rooted plane trees of n+1 nodes.

The path reading above and the tree reading are two faces of the same word, and they disagree on shape. The path's area ranks the nested word <math>x x \dots x \overline{x} \overline{x} \dots \overline{x}</math> lowest and the flat alternating word highest, while the tree records nesting exactly. Area has no native meaning on a tree, and depth has none on a path.

A Lisp S-expression is a plane tree, and its parenthesis skeleton is a Dyck word. See [[Dyck Words/Lisp]].

===Steep Dyck Words===

A Dyck word is steep if it is nonempty and contains no <math>x \overline{x} x</math> factor (no up-down-up). In path terms, a southeast step is never sandwiched between two northeast steps: every down step is preceded by a down step, followed by a down step, or is the final step.

The default path <math>x x \dots x \overline{x} \overline{x} \dots \overline{x}</math> from the definitions above is itself steep: it is the extreme case, a single climb followed by a single descent.

To count steep parallelogram polyominoes, use the [[Motzkin Numbers|Motzkin numbers]], which count them by perimeter.

There is a classical bijection between parallelogram polyominoes and Dyck words; object grammars explain it, and yield a functional equation for the generating function of steep polyominoes by width, perimeter, and area.

Let <math>G_{SW}(x,q)</math> be the steep Dyck word generating function by inversion number q and length x.

Via q-grammars, the generating function of steep Dyck words of length 2n, counted by inversion number, equals the (n-1)th q-Motzkin number <math>M_{n-1}(q)</math>:

<math>
G_{SW}(1,x,q) = x \sum_{n \geq 0} M_n (q) x^n
</math>

Start from the grammar for nonempty Dyck words:

<math>
D^{\prime} \rightarrow x \overline{x} | x \overline{x} D^{\prime} | x D^{\prime} \overline{x} | x D^{\prime} \overline{x} D^{\prime}
</math>

The forbidden <math>x \overline{x} x</math> sequence is produced only by the second rule,

<math>
D^{\prime} \rightarrow x \overline{x} D^{\prime}
</math>

so the steep Dyck words are generated by the grammar with that rule removed:

<math>
S \rightarrow x \overline{x} | x S \overline{x} | x S \overline{x} S
</math>

Letting <math>G_{SW}(x) = \sum_{n \geq 1} S_n x^n</math>, where <math>S_n</math> counts steep Dyck words of length 2n, read off

<math>
G_{SW}(x) = x + x G_{SW}(x) + x G_{SW}(x)^2
</math>

so steep Dyck words of length 2n are enumerated by the (n-1)th Motzkin number.

Getting the q-refinement requires the q-analog <math>(w;q)</math> of a Dyck word and q-grammars.

===Generalizing Dyck Grammars===

The first-return grammar generalizes: change the steps and the same decomposition still builds words. In [[Project Euler/502]] the up and right movements are split into <code>U</code> (up one row), <code>R</code> (right one column), and <code>D</code> (down one row), and a castle tower is a word over these that stays above the base and returns to it. The castle rules re-cast as a grammar with the same first-return split, and reading off its generating function yields the recurrence that counts them. See [[Project Euler/502/Representations#Generalized Dyck Grammar for Castles|Generalized Dyck Grammar for Castles]].
